earlier_scan.source_named: OLAC lists no descriptive resources at all for Nungu/Rindre beyond Ethnologue/LINGUIST List stubs; no wordlist, grammar or phonology located (rogerblench.info also empty for Rindre).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2006. The Nunku language of Central Nigeria and its affinities (draft wordlist paper; data collected by Barau Kato 2003).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: NOT this language: Nunku is a member of the Numana-Nunku-Gwantu-Numbu cluster (Atlas ed. III, entry 343), not Nungu/Rindre. Opened only to rule out the name confusion; it has a §3.3 Tones section and no stress remarks. Not counted as a Nungu source.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. Research on the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 3-44. doi:10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.209
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Nungu phonology. §2.4 Ninzic (p. 24): 'Descriptive materials on Ninzic are sparse'; specific-language materials named are Hoffmann 1976, Hörner 1980 (Ninzam), Price 1989 (Mada), Ninzo LPC 1999, Wilson 2003 (Kuche), Blench & Kato in progress (Mada) — none for Nungu. Nungu figures only in the classification table (Table 3) and in the note that Shimizu 1975a used it lexicostatistically. No 'stress'/'accent' anywhere in the article.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2012. An Atlas of Nigerian Languages, 3rd ed. (version 03 Dec 2012). Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. Entry 386 'Rindre'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Entry 386 Rindre: names Rendre, Rindiri, Lindiri; Wamba, Nungu; Nasarawa State, Akwanga LGA; 10,000 (1972 Welmers), 25,000 (SIL); Benue-Congo: Plateau: Ninzic; dialects Rindre, Gudi; second language Hausa; 'Source(s) Kato (2008)'. No linguistic description, no literacy materials listed.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. n.d. (page dated 2011/2015). Ninzic languages: wordlists & papers. Web page, rogerblench.info (the Internet Archive 2025-05-28).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Index page only. Lists wordlists for Anib, Ayu, Bu, Ce, Mada, Ningye, Ninka, Ninkyop, Ninzo, Numana, Nunku — no Rindre/Nungu item. (The 'Nunku' wordlist is a different language, see next row.) Confirms the earlier scan note that Blench's site has nothing for Rindre.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2008. Prospecting proto-Plateau. Ms. (rogerblench.info, the Internet Archive 2025-05-28).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Nungu appears only as a row in classification tables and in two comparative lexical sets (mekru, ubye); no phonological description; 'stress'/'accent' absent.

sources.citation: Mathews, H. F. 1917. Notes on the Nungu tribe, Nassawara Province, Northern Nigeria, and the neighboring tribes which use the duodecimal system of numeration. Harvard African Studies 1: 83-93.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic notes plus a comparative table of numerals 1-12+ for Nungu, South Mada, Mama and Ninzam (pp. 92-93); the author says he could not collect large vocabularies; no remarks on accent, tone or pronunciation of Nungu.

sources.citation: Wikipedia 'Nungu language'; Wikidata Q3913350; Wikitongues rin; Joshua Project Nungu/Rindre profile; ISO 639-3 rin record.
sources.note: Nothing. Wikipedia is a stub citing Ethnologue (dialects Rinde/Rindre and Gudi, ~30,000 speakers 1999); Wikitongues lists no resources; Joshua Project: Bible translation 'started', Global Recordings audio only. Ethnologue, SIL resources, OLAC and language-archives.org were blocked/unreachable.

sources.citation: Eberhard, Simons & Fennig (eds.). 2025. Ethnologue, 28th ed.: entry 'Nungu' [rin]; plus SIL Nigeria resources for rin.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: publisher DOI, paywalled; library e-access not checked
sources.note: Might list a Rindre orthography/literacy document or survey report (Joshua Project reports a Bible translation 'started', so an orthography statement may exist)

sources.citation: Kato, Barau. 2008. Rindre wordlist / field notes (unpublished; sole source named for the Rindre entry in Blench, Atlas of Nigerian Languages ed. III, entry 386).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Only known primary field data on Rindre; Blench/Kato wordlist papers normally carry a short phonology with a Tones section, so this is the one item likely to say whether the language is tonal and whether stress plays any role.

sources.citation: Gerhardt, Ludwig. 1983. Beiträge zur Kenntnis der Sprachen des Nigerianischen Plateaus. Glückstadt: J.J. Augustin.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The main descriptive work on Plateau (Greenberg's groups 2 and 4) noun-class languages; whether it contains any Nungu material is unverified (Nungu was Plateau 5 in the older classification, so probably not), but it is the only substantial descriptive monograph on the neighbouring Ninzic languages.

sources.citation: Shimizu, Kiyoshi. 1975. A lexicostatistical study of Plateau languages and Jukun. Anthropological Linguistics 17(9): 413-418.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: publisher DOI, paywalled; library e-access not checked
sources.note: Used Nungu data; lexicostatistics only, so low chance of a stress remark, but it is one of the few published works with Nungu forms.

sources.citation: Williamson, Kay & Kiyoshi Shimizu (eds.). 1968. Benue-Congo Comparative Wordlist, vol. I; Williamson, Kay (ed.). 1973. vol. II. Ibadan: West African Linguistic Society.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Contains a tone-marked Nungu (Lindiri) wordlist — the only published lexical data; would establish tonal status (no stress statement expected, but it is the primary data any phonology would start from).
